title: Global Summit: Trade Negotiations
description: India has been invited to host a major international trade summit in New Delhi. You are Vikram Mehta, India's lead trade negotiator at the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Representatives from the USA, EU, China, Japan, and African Union are at the table. Each wants something different -- market access, technology transfer, agricultural protections, or strategic alliances. Your mission: negotiate the best deals for India while building lasting international partnerships. Manage your influence, trust, trade balance, and alliances as you navigate the complex world of global diplomacy. Can you make India a central player in the new global economic order?
learning_objectives: Understand the basics of international trade, tariffs, and trade agreements
Learn about India's position in global trade organizations (WTO, BRICS, G20)
Develop negotiation skills: compromise, leverage, and win-win strategies
Explore the tension between protectionism and free trade in the Indian context
Understand geopolitics, strategic alliances, and India's 'multi-alignment' foreign policy

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are India's lead trade negotiator at a major international summit in New Delhi
Each round presents a negotiation scenario with a different country or group
Choose your negotiation strategy: aggressive, cooperative, or strategic
Monitor your Influence, Trust, Trade Balance (INR), and Allies Count
Building trust enables better deals later; burning bridges closes doors
Aim to maximize India's trade benefits while maintaining strong international relationships
tips: Trust is the currency of diplomacy -- once lost, it is very hard to rebuild
Every deal has trade-offs; there are no perfect agreements in international negotiations
Allies count is not just about numbers -- the right allies at the right time matter most
India's size and market give it natural leverage; use it wisely, not aggressively
Study each country's priorities before choosing your approach -- good negotiators listen first

rounds.title: Round 1: The Opening Gambit -- Setting India's Agenda
rounds.story: The summit opens in Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi. As the host nation, India gets to set the agenda. The world is watching -- 42 countries are represented, and India's G20 presidency has given it unprecedented visibility. You must decide India's opening position. The Commerce Secretary advises caution, the PM wants bold moves, and the industry lobby wants maximum market protection. How you frame India's priorities in the opening session will shape every negotiation that follows.
rounds.goal: Set India's negotiating agenda to maximize leverage while building goodwill as the host nation.

choices.label: Propose 'Inclusive Trade' -- Focus on Developing Nations
choices.feedback: You position India as the voice of the Global South, proposing trade rules that benefit developing nations. African and ASEAN delegates applaud. India's leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement and its role in founding G77 give this position historical weight. At the WTO, India has consistently championed Special and Differential Treatment for developing countries. This builds enormous goodwill and alliances but may face resistance from wealthy nations who prefer different rules.

choices.label: Push for Bilateral Deals -- India-First Approach
choices.feedback: You propose bilateral trade agreements where India can negotiate from strength with individual countries. This is pragmatic -- India's massive consumer market (1.4 billion people) gives it strong bilateral leverage. India has existing bilateral agreements with Japan, South Korea, and ASEAN. However, smaller nations feel excluded and the 'India-First' framing generates some unease. Bilateral deals can be efficient but may undermine the multilateral system that protects smaller economies.

choices.label: Champion Digital Trade and Technology Partnership
choices.feedback: You propose a Digital Trade Framework highlighting India's strengths: the world's largest digital payments ecosystem (UPI), massive IT services sector, and growing startup ecosystem. India processed 89 billion UPI transactions in 2023, and Indian IT exports exceed $150 billion. By championing digital trade, you position India at the frontier of the new economy. The EU and Japan are interested; China is wary. Your tech-forward agenda establishes India as a 21st-century economic power, not just a developing nation.

rounds.image_prompt: a grand conference room in Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi, adorned with flags of 42 nations, delegates seated at a large oval table, intense discussions under bright overhead lights
rounds.coaching_moment: In multilateral negotiations, agenda-setting is itself a power move. The country that defines the frame of the debate determines which outcomes are even imaginable. India's 'Voice of the Global South' summit in 2023 was precisely this: not a negotiation yet, but a pre-negotiation maneuver to shift what developed nations would have to defend. The choice of where to open determines which concessions you'll be asked to make versus which ones you'll be in a position to demand.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 2: The American Demand -- Market Access
rounds.story: The US Trade Representative pulls you aside for a bilateral meeting. She wants India to reduce tariffs on American dairy products, medical devices, and tech hardware. In return, the US offers increased H-1B visa allocations and defense technology sharing. India's dairy tariffs protect 80 million dairy farmers (the world's largest dairy sector), and reducing them could devastate livelihoods. But H-1B visas and defense tech are hugely valuable. The US hints that without a deal, India's GSP (Generalized System of Preferences) reinstatement is unlikely.
rounds.goal: Negotiate with the United States, balancing farmer protection with access to technology and visas.

choices.label: Firmly Protect Dairy Farmers -- Reject Tariff Reduction
choices.feedback: You cite India's food security concerns and the livelihoods of 80 million dairy farmers. India's dairy cooperative movement (Amul/GCMMF), started by Dr. Verghese Kurien, made India the world's largest milk producer. The WTO's Agreement on Agriculture allows developing countries special protections for food security. Your firm stance protects farmers but strains the US relationship. India withdrew from RCEP in 2019 over similar agricultural concerns -- protecting farmers is a consistent Indian trade policy position.

choices.label: Propose Phased Tariff Reduction Over 10 Years
choices.feedback: You propose a gradual tariff reduction with safeguard clauses: if imports surge beyond a threshold, tariffs snap back automatically. This is a standard WTO-compliant mechanism. You also insist on reciprocal market access for Indian pharmaceutical generics in the US market. India produces 60% of the world's vaccines and 20% of global generic medicines. A phased approach gives Indian dairy farmers time to modernize while gaining valuable concessions. Good negotiation creates time for adjustment, not sudden shocks.

choices.label: Counter-Offer: Open Tech but Protect Agriculture Completely
choices.feedback: You offer to reduce tariffs on American tech hardware and medical devices (benefiting Indian consumers and hospitals) while keeping agricultural tariffs intact. In exchange, you demand technology transfer agreements and joint manufacturing under Make in India. This is the 'sectoral approach' -- opening sectors where India benefits from imports while protecting sensitive sectors. India's $100 billion medical device market and growing tech hardware demand make this a credible offer that serves Indian interests while giving America something real.

rounds.image_prompt: a grand conference room filled with polished wooden tables and flags from both nations, officials in suits engaged in a heated discussion, a projector displaying trade graphs in the background
rounds.coaching_moment: Your BATNA — Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement — determines your floor, but your relationships determine your ceiling. India's agricultural sector represents 150 million farming households whose livelihoods depend on import protection that no WTO round has ever successfully dismantled. Understanding the American domestic politics behind the demand (farm lobbies, trade adjustment pressure) helps India find the offer that gives the US a headline win while protecting what cannot be conceded.

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: Round 3: The EU Carbon Border Tax Standoff
rounds.story: The European Union delegates present their Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) -- a tax on imports based on their carbon footprint. India's steel and aluminium exports to Europe (worth $8 billion annually) would face a 15-20% additional tariff. The EU argues this levels the playing field and fights climate change. India argues it is disguised protectionism that punishes developing nations who did not cause the climate crisis. Brazil, South Africa, and ASEAN nations look to India for leadership on this issue.
rounds.goal: Navigate the complex intersection of climate policy and trade fairness, defending India's interests while acknowledging environmental responsibility.

choices.label: Lead a Coalition Against CBAM as Climate Colonialism
choices.feedback: You rally developing nations against CBAM, arguing it violates the UNFCCC principle of 'Common But Differentiated Responsibilities.' India's per-capita emissions are one-third the global average and one-tenth of America's. Historically, developed nations caused 80% of cumulative emissions. India has consistently argued at COP summits that climate action cannot punish those least responsible. Your coalition is powerful -- 90 nations support your position -- but the EU is determined. The battle lines are drawn.

choices.label: Negotiate Exemptions for India + Joint Green Technology Fund
choices.feedback: You propose that CBAM revenues from Indian exports be recycled into a joint India-EU Green Technology Fund, helping Indian industries decarbonize. You also seek a 7-year exemption period for Indian MSMEs. This mirrors India's approach at COP26 -- accepting net-zero targets by 2070 while demanding climate finance from developed nations. Creative negotiation finds a third way between rejection and acceptance. The EU appreciates India's constructive approach, and the Fund becomes a model for North-South climate cooperation.

choices.label: Announce India's Own Carbon Trading Scheme
choices.feedback: You announce that India is launching its own Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (already approved under the Energy Conservation Amendment Act, 2022) and demand mutual recognition with EU's ETS. If India has its own carbon pricing, CBAM becomes redundant for Indian goods. India's International Solar Alliance, National Hydrogen Mission, and target of 500 GW renewable energy by 2030 demonstrate genuine climate commitment. By matching the EU's mechanism with an Indian equivalent, you neutralize their trade advantage while accelerating India's green transition.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling conference room filled with European Union delegates at a grand table, papers and laptops scattered, intense discussions under bright overhead lights, a world map on the wall
rounds.coaching_moment: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism is simultaneously a climate instrument and a trade barrier — and the EU's refusal to acknowledge the second makes it a negotiating flashpoint. India's per-capita emissions remain one-eighth of the EU's; invoking the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities' from the Paris Agreement is legally grounded, not just rhetorical. The strongest negotiating positions connect moral authority to practical alternatives — building a coalition is more powerful than bilateral objection.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you choose this option? What were you trying to protect or grow?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 4: The China Question -- Competing and Cooperating
rounds.story: China proposes a BRICS trade facilitation agreement that would reduce tariffs among BRICS nations (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa). The deal would give Indian exporters access to China's $18 trillion economy but also flood India with cheap Chinese goods. India already has a $85 billion trade deficit with China. Indian manufacturers fear they cannot compete with China's scale and subsidies. However, rejecting BRICS cooperation could push India's other BRICS partners closer to China. The geopolitical and economic stakes are enormous.
rounds.goal: Navigate the complex India-China trade relationship, balancing economic protection with strategic engagement.

choices.label: Accept Selectively -- Open Only Sectors Where India Excels
choices.feedback: You propose sectoral opening: India reduces tariffs on Chinese raw materials and machinery (inputs for Indian manufacturing) while China opens markets for Indian pharmaceuticals, IT services, and agricultural products. India's pharma exports are already valued at $25 billion, and IT services at $150 billion. Selective engagement maximizes India's comparative advantages. This approach reflects India's PLI (Production Linked Incentive) scheme strategy -- build domestic capacity first, then compete globally. Smart trade policy is not about closing doors but choosing which ones to open.

choices.label: Reject the BRICS Deal -- Protect Indian Manufacturing
choices.feedback: You firmly decline, citing India's $85 billion trade deficit with China and the need to develop domestic manufacturing under Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat. India withdrew from RCEP in 2019 partly because of similar concerns about Chinese imports. Your stance protects Indian SMEs but isolates India within BRICS. Brazil and South Africa move closer to China. In trade diplomacy, saying no preserves autonomy but can reduce relevance. The challenge is protecting your economy without isolating your diplomacy.

choices.label: Agree With Strict Conditions -- Anti-Dumping + Rules of Origin
choices.feedback: You accept the framework but insist on robust anti-dumping mechanisms, strict rules of origin (preventing Chinese goods from routing through third countries), and a dispute resolution mechanism. India's Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) handles anti-dumping cases -- India files among the most anti-dumping cases globally at the WTO. Conditional engagement is sophisticated diplomacy: you stay at the table, maintain alliances, and protect domestic industry through legal mechanisms rather than outright rejection.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant marketplace bustling with vendors showcasing colorful goods, banners of BRICS nations hanging overhead, sunlight filtering through canopies, a hint of tension in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: Trade negotiations with a strategic competitor require separating economic calculus from geopolitical signaling. India's trade deficit with China crossed $85 billion in 2023, yet Chinese inputs are embedded throughout Indian manufacturing supply chains. The art is selective engagement: identifying the sectors where Indian capability is strongest and opening those, while using anti-dumping mechanisms for sectors where Chinese state subsidies would otherwise crowd out domestic industry.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 5: The African Partnership -- South-South Cooperation
rounds.story: The African Union delegation approaches you with a comprehensive proposal: they want Indian investment in African manufacturing, technology transfer for pharmaceutical production, and agricultural expertise. In return, they offer preferential access to African mineral resources critical for India's electronics and renewable energy sectors (lithium, cobalt, rare earths). Africa's 1.4 billion population is the world's fastest-growing consumer market. China has invested heavily in Africa; India's presence is much smaller. This could be India's opportunity to build a lasting partnership.
rounds.goal: Design India's partnership with Africa that is mutually beneficial and avoids the exploitative patterns of traditional North-South engagement.

choices.label: Propose 'India-Africa Partnership 2.0' -- All-Encompassing
choices.feedback: You propose a comprehensive partnership: Indian pharma companies set up manufacturing in Africa (making medicines locally), IIT-trained engineers build solar farms, Indian agricultural universities share drought-resistant crop technology, and Africa provides mineral access and market entry. India's existing Duty-Free Tariff Preference (DFTP) scheme already covers 34 African LDCs. This partnership model -- based on capacity building rather than extraction -- reflects India's South-South cooperation philosophy championed since the Bandung Conference (1955).

choices.label: Focus on Pharmaceutical and Health Partnership
choices.feedback: You propose that Indian pharma companies build factories in Africa to produce generic medicines and vaccines locally. India already supplies 50-80% of Africa's generic medicines. The Serum Institute of India produces 1.5 billion vaccine doses annually. During COVID-19, India's Vaccine Maitri initiative supplied millions of doses to African nations. Health diplomacy builds deep trust because it directly saves lives. Africa's 'Pharma Africa' initiative aligns perfectly with India's pharmaceutical strengths. This partnership could save millions of lives while building lasting economic ties.

choices.label: Prioritize Critical Mineral Access for India's Tech Sector
choices.feedback: You negotiate preferential access to African lithium, cobalt, and rare earth minerals essential for India's electronics, EV battery, and semiconductor manufacturing ambitions. India's KABIL (Khanij Bidesh India Limited) was created specifically for overseas mineral acquisition. However, a minerals-first approach risks looking extractive -- similar to criticisms of China's Africa strategy. India's soft power in Africa (Bollywood, cricket, Indian diaspora, democratic values) is an asset, but it only works if partnerships feel equal. Resource diplomacy must be paired with genuine development partnerships.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant conference room filled with diverse delegates engaged in animated discussions, a large map of Africa on the wall, sunlight streaming through large windows, a feeling of collaboration and opportunity
rounds.coaching_moment: South-South cooperation between India and Africa is not charity — it is strategic statecraft. India's pharmaceutical exports to Africa already account for over 50% of Africa's generic medicine needs. The question is whether to deepen a single high-value partnership or spread India's presence broadly. Concentrated partnerships build deeper relationships and reliable allies; broad partnerships signal solidarity and reduce dependency on any single country's goodwill.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How might the people affected by this choice experience the outcome?

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: Round 6: The Intellectual Property Battle
rounds.story: A contentious session erupts over intellectual property rights. The US and EU demand India strengthen patent protections, particularly for pharmaceuticals. India's compulsory licensing provisions (Section 3(d) of the Indian Patent Act) allow it to produce affordable generic versions of expensive patented drugs -- this saves millions of lives globally but costs Western pharma companies billions. The landmark Novartis v. Union of India case (2013) upheld India's right to do this. Now, it is under attack in the trade negotiations. Global health NGOs are watching closely.
rounds.goal: Defend India's pharmaceutical innovation model while maintaining trade relationships with countries demanding stricter IP rules.

choices.label: Firmly Defend Section 3(d) -- Lives Over Profits
choices.feedback: You cite the WTO's Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health, which affirms countries' rights to protect public health. India's generic pharma industry supplies affordable medicines to over 100 countries. The Supreme Court's Novartis judgment was a landmark in balancing patent rights with public health. You argue that India's Section 3(d) prevents 'evergreening' -- the practice of making minor changes to existing drugs to extend patent monopolies. Your firm defense earns you allies among developing nations and global health organizations, but Western pharma companies lobby their governments harder.

choices.label: Propose Enhanced Data Exclusivity with Public Health Exceptions
choices.feedback: You offer limited data exclusivity (5 years instead of the demanded 12) with clear exceptions for public health emergencies, compulsory licensing for cancer and HIV drugs, and mandatory technology transfer provisions. India's Department of Pharmaceuticals has been exploring balanced IP frameworks. This middle path shows flexibility while protecting India's core interests. The EU and Japan are more receptive than the US. In diplomacy, the willingness to negotiate details while holding firm on principles is the hallmark of skilled statecraft.

choices.label: Reframe the Debate -- India as Innovation Hub, Not Just Generics
choices.feedback: You highlight that India is not just a generics producer -- it is increasingly an innovator. India ranks 40th on the Global Innovation Index, has the 3rd largest startup ecosystem globally, and Indian pharma companies are developing novel drugs and biosimilars. You propose a Global Innovation Fund where IP revenues are shared with countries that invest in R&D. India's IT and pharma sectors prove that innovation and affordability can coexist. Reframing India from 'copycat' to 'innovator' changes the entire power dynamic in IP negotiations.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant conference room filled with diverse delegates at a long table, animated discussions underway, papers and laptops scattered, a large screen displaying patent graphics, tension in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: India's Section 3(d) of the Patent Act — which denies patents for incremental modifications of known compounds — has been called the 'gold standard of public health flexibilities' by MSF. It exists because millions of Indians access HIV, TB, and cancer medicines at one-tenth the cost of patented versions. In IP negotiations, the frame matters: 'protecting innovation' is the developed-world frame; 'preventing monopoly abuse' is India's frame. The strongest position refuses to negotiate within the opponent's frame.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back, do you think this was the best use of your resources?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 7: The Currency and Digital Payments Proposal
rounds.story: India proposes that the summit endorse UPI (Unified Payments Interface) as a model for global digital payment interoperability. India's UPI processed 12 billion transactions in a single month, far exceeding any other country's digital payment system. Singapore and UAE have already linked their payment systems with UPI. This could reduce dependence on SWIFT and the US dollar for international transactions. The US delegation is uncomfortable -- dollar dominance is a cornerstone of American economic power. China offers to co-develop an alternative with India using their own digital yuan. Russia supports de-dollarisation enthusiastically.
rounds.goal: Navigate the sensitive geopolitics of international currency and payment systems while advancing India's digital leadership.

choices.label: Push for UPI as Global Standard -- India Leads
choices.feedback: You present UPI's achievements: 300 million users, near-zero transaction costs, financial inclusion for millions of previously unbanked Indians. NPCI International is already expanding UPI to 20+ countries. You propose a 'Global Payment Interconnect' based on UPI's open architecture. India's JAM Trinity (Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile) created the world's most successful financial inclusion programme. By proposing an open standard (unlike China's closed system), India positions itself as a democratic alternative in digital finance. The EU and Japan express strong interest.

choices.label: Expand UPI Through Bilateral Links (Less Controversial)
choices.feedback: Rather than challenging the dollar system directly, you propose bilateral UPI linkages with willing countries. India already has such agreements with Singapore, UAE, France, and others. This incremental approach avoids geopolitical confrontation while steadily building India's digital payment ecosystem globally. RBI's approach to internationalising the rupee has similarly been gradual -- allowing rupee trade settlement with 22 countries. Incremental diplomacy avoids backlash while achieving the same long-term goal.

choices.label: Propose Multi-Currency Digital Platform Through BRICS
choices.feedback: You propose a BRICS-backed multi-currency digital payment platform where each nation uses its own currency. This excites Russia (facing SWIFT sanctions) and China (pushing the digital yuan) but deeply concerns the US and EU. De-dollarisation is one of the most sensitive geopolitical topics globally. India's approach must be careful -- it benefits from both the Western financial system and BRICS solidarity. The New Development Bank (BRICS Bank) in Shanghai already offers local currency financing. Multi-alignment means not picking sides but maximising options.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant summit conference room with representatives from various countries seated around a large oval table, digital screens displaying UPI statistics, sunlight streaming through tall windows, a tense atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: UPI processed over 14 billion transactions in January 2024 alone — India has built the world's most advanced public digital payments infrastructure. Proposing UPI as a global standard is audacious because it asks the world to adopt India's architecture rather than adapting Indian systems to SWIFT. The risk is overreach: bilateral UPI links with Singapore, UAE, and France have succeeded precisely because they were consensual and mutual. The question is whether the G20 moment justifies the ambition of a global push.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is this decision optimizing for short-term or long-term outcomes? Which matters more here?

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: Round 8: The Grand Finale -- Signing the Delhi Declaration
rounds.story: After days of intense negotiations, it is time to craft the final Delhi Declaration -- a joint statement that will define global trade cooperation for the next decade. Three competing visions are on the table. The declaration India signs will signal its global economic direction. The PM calls you: 'Make India proud, but make India wise. We want to be a leader, not just a follower of anyone's rules.' The world is watching as India, for the first time, hosts a trade summit of this magnitude and crafts the outcome document.
rounds.goal: Craft the final Delhi Declaration that maximises India's interests while creating a lasting framework for fair global trade.

choices.label: Delhi Declaration: Balanced Multilateralism with Indian Characteristics
choices.feedback: Your declaration balances free trade with fair trade: reduced tariffs for manufactured goods, protected food security for developing nations, digital trade standards based on interoperability (not monopoly), and a climate-trade mechanism that respects differentiated responsibilities. India's successful G20 presidency demonstrated that India can lead balanced global consensus. The Delhi Declaration is compared to the Bandung Declaration (1955) and becomes a reference document for future trade negotiations. India emerges as a bridge between North and South, East and West.

choices.label: Delhi Declaration: Bold Vision for Global South Leadership
choices.feedback: Your declaration centres the Global South: restructured WTO voting (giving developing nations more voice), mandatory technology transfer for climate adaptation, agricultural protection rights, and a Development Finance Facility. 134 developing nations co-sign. India's voice in Nehru's tradition of Non-Alignment evolves into active leadership of the Global South. This bold vision establishes India as the undisputed leader of developing nations but creates tension with the G7. India's PM called this being 'Vishwaguru' (world teacher) -- a teacher must sometimes challenge the powerful to protect the vulnerable.

choices.label: Delhi Declaration: Pragmatic Deals Over Grand Statements
choices.feedback: You opt for concrete bilateral and plurilateral deals over a grand multilateral declaration. India signs FTAs with the EU (after 16 years of negotiation), a technology partnership with Japan, a mineral access agreement with the African Union, and a digital trade framework with ASEAN. Pragmatism over idealism. India's trade policy has been shifting this direction -- the India-Australia ECTA and India-UAE CEPA were concluded remarkably fast. Concrete deals deliver immediate economic benefits. The Delhi Summit is remembered not for rhetoric but for results.

choices.label: Delhi Declaration: Future-Forward Innovation and Sustainability Pact
choices.feedback: Your declaration focuses on the future: AI governance standards, space commerce rules, green hydrogen trade corridors, digital public goods sharing (like India's open-source DPI stack), and a Global Startup Exchange programme. India's Digital Public Infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker, CoWIN) has been praised by the World Bank and IMF as a model. By focusing on innovation and sustainability, you position India at the cutting edge of 21st-century trade. The Delhi Innovation Pact becomes the foundation for a new era of technology-driven global cooperation.

rounds.image_prompt: a grand conference hall filled with delegates from around the world, flags representing various nations, a large round table with papers and laptops, bright spotlight illuminating the scene, intense focus in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: The language of a multilateral declaration is itself a negotiation — every adjective is contested, every comma is a compromise. India's G20 presidency in 2023 succeeded by finding language on Ukraine that all parties could sign without losing face, replacing 'aggression' with 'the war in Ukraine.' A grand declaration that all parties sign is diplomatically more valuable than a bold statement that fractures the coalition. The art of the final communique is making everyone feel they won something real.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If this were a real business decision, what extra information would you want?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

glossary_terms.definition: An international organization headquartered in Geneva that regulates and facilitates international trade. India is a founding member. The WTO's agreements cover goods, services, and intellectual property, and its dispute settlement mechanism is often called the 'backbone' of the global trading system.

A tax imposed on imported goods. Tariffs protect domestic industries from foreign competition but raise prices for consumers. India's average tariff rate is around 18%, higher than most developed countries. Tariff negotiations are at the heart of every trade deal.

An intergovernmental organization comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa (expanded in 2024 to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and UAE). Originally an economic grouping, BRICS now coordinates on trade, finance, and geopolitical issues, representing over 40% of the world's population.

India's real-time payment system developed by NPCI that enables instant money transfers between bank accounts via mobile phones. Processing over 10 billion monthly transactions, UPI has been internationally recognized as the world's most successful digital payment infrastructure.

A preferential tariff system extended by developed countries to developing nations. The US withdrew India's GSP benefits in 2019 affecting $6.3 billion in exports. GSP reinstatement is a recurring topic in India-US trade negotiations.
